WHY IT HAS TO EXIST

The appeal usually wins.
Almost nobody files it.

The most damning numbers in insurance are the appeal rates. The system works for those who push back, and almost no one is equipped to.

F·01

The unfiled appeal

US marketplace data analysed by KFF shows claimants appeal under 1% of denied in-network claims. Where they do, a large share of appeals succeed, in some datasets between four and six-plus out of every ten. The gap between those numbers is the product.

F·02

Denial at machine speed

ProPublica reported a major US insurer’s review system enabling denials at an average of 1.2 seconds per claim across hundreds of thousands of claims. In any jurisdiction, the direction is clear: the assessing side is automated.

F·03

Europe’s numbers agree

The UK Financial Ombudsman upholds roughly a third of insurance complaints brought to it, higher in some categories. Germany’s BaFin logged a sharp surge in insurance complaints. Pushing back works; people need the means.

F·04

The paperwork is the weapon

Deadlines, evidence formats, policy exclusions in defined terms: the process itself deters claimants, and the attrition is the point.

For the side of the table
without a claims department.

The denied policyholder

The first user holds a denial letter and a sense of injustice, and is about to give up. The Advocate’s job is that moment: decode the denial against the actual policy wording, assess what an appeal needs, assemble it properly, and know when the ombudsman is the next stop.

WHAT IT CHANGES

From shoebox
to case file.

The Advocate provides information and document support: decoding, organising, drafting for your review. It does not give legal advice, and it tells you plainly when a matter needs an ombudsman, a regulated advisor or a lawyer.

The policy, decoded.

Your own wording (cover, exclusions, defined terms, deadlines) explained in plain language against the facts of your claim.

The file, built properly.

The Advocate collects, orders and gap-checks your evidence into the shape claim handlers process fastest, and drafts appeal letters for your approval, grounded in the policy text.

The escalation map.

The Advocate tracks the deadlines and queues the next step along each jurisdiction’s free routes: internal complaint, ombudsman, regulator.

THE MECHANICS

Document intelligence,
with a compliance spine.

The core is careful document work (reading policies, structuring evidence, drafting correspondence) wrapped in a boundary layer that keeps the tool on the right side of legal-services and claims-management rules in each market it enters.

Every VF system runs on the harness stack, is steered by the Helmsman engine and is watched from a command dashboard.

LAYER 1

The policy reader

Extraction and plain-language explanation of cover, exclusions, conditions and time limits from the policyholder’s own documents, with each explanation anchored to the clause it came from.

LAYER 2

The evidence organiser

Photos, reports, invoices and correspondence, structured into a chronological, gap-checked case file that both sides of the table can read.

LAYER 3

The drafting engine

Appeal and complaint correspondence generated from policy text and evidence, always for the claimant’s review and signature. The tool prepares; the claimant speaks.

LAYER 4

The boundary layer

Jurisdiction-aware rules for what the tool may and may not do, with routing to ombudsman schemes, regulated claims professionals and lawyers built in as a feature.

QUESTIONS

Asked.
Answered.

Is Claims Advocate legal advice?

No. It provides information and document support: decoding, organising and drafting for your review. A jurisdiction-aware boundary layer keeps the tool on the right side of legal-services and claims-management rules in each market, and it tells you plainly when a matter needs an ombudsman, a regulated advisor or a lawyer.

What does it do with my denial letter?

It decodes the denial against your actual policy wording: cover, exclusions, defined terms and deadlines explained in plain language, each explanation anchored to the clause it came from. It then assesses what an appeal needs, assembles your evidence into a chronological, gap-checked case file and drafts appeal letters for your approval.

Which claims does it cover?

Household and property claims first: water, storm, fire, burglary. Motor, travel and health claim support follow, then small-business claims such as business interruption and commercial property. Health and disability claimants get structured support with routing to professionals and advice services where matters exceed a tool.

Does it know the ombudsman route?

Yes. The Advocate tracks deadlines and queues the next step along each jurisdiction’s free routes: internal complaint, ombudsman, regulator. Routing to ombudsman schemes, regulated claims professionals and lawyers is built in as a feature, and VF will maintain the escalation-route directory in the open.

When does it ship?

Claims Advocate is in build. The property core comes first: policy decoding, case-file assembly and appeal drafting proven on real denials in the pilot jurisdictions. Motor, travel and health lines follow with deadline automation and ombudsman-format exports, then general availability across initial EU markets and the UK. Real cases shape the pilot.
